claim: Of the 216 individual Debian package maintainers active at Debian release 2.0 (July 1998), only 121 (55.8%) were still contributing maintainers 6.5 years later at the Debian 3.1 candidate release (December 2004).
stance_target: open-source volunteer contributor communities have a documented, person-level, multi-year cohort-survival curve directly analogous to a creator/channel attrition curve
scope_conditions: Debian project package maintainers only; July 1998 to December 2004 (6.5 years)
quoted_support: the number decreases steadily, with only 121 of the original 216 contributors (55.8%) still contributing to Debian in December 2004.

claim: The authors estimate a contributor half-life (time for a maintainer cohort to fall to half its initial population) of approximately 7.5 years (90 months) for Debian package maintainers, extrapolated from the observed 6.5-year decay trend, and note the same half-life estimate holds regardless of which release is chosen as the starting cohort.
stance_target: there exists a quantified half-life/survival-curve figure for open-source volunteer contributors that can serve as a cross-domain comparison point for creator-platform attrition
scope_conditions: Debian package maintainers, extrapolated from 1998-2004 data
quoted_support: the number of maintainers from previous releases who remain active is very high, with an estimated half-life of around 7.5 years (90 months). More than half of the maintainers from Debian 2.0 still contribute to the current release.

claim: Debian's total individual-maintainer population grew from 216 (Jul 1998) to about 1,237 (Dec 2004), roughly 35% per year, even while the specific 1998 cohort of maintainers was steadily attriting -- illustrating that aggregate headline-count growth can mask substantial cohort-level attrition.
stance_target: aggregate platform/community growth figures do not reveal underlying cohort attrition, which is exactly the telemetry gap the research question is probing
quoted_support: the number of Debian individual maintainers has been growing in time. 2.0 (July 1998) was put together by 216 individual maintainers, while the number of maintainers for later releases are 859 for 3.0 (July 2002) and will be of about 1,237 for 3.1 (December 2004). This shows a growth of about 35% every year.

claim: Software packages orphaned when a Debian maintainer leaves the project are adopted by another maintainer more than 60% of the time across every studied release-pair, evidencing a project-level 'regeneration' process that offsets individual-level attrition.
stance_target: project-level continuity survives despite substantial individual contributor attrition (the 7.5-year half-life)
scope_conditions: Debian, all release pairs from 2.0 (1998) to 3.1 candidate (2004)
quoted_support: the percentage of adopted packages is very high: more than 60% for all releases considered... we can thus affirm that Debian counts on a natural 'regeneration' process for its voluntary contributors
numbers: >60% adoption rate across all release pairs

claim: Debian maintainers who remain active accumulate more responsibility over time: the surviving 1998 cohort's packages-per-maintainer ratio rose from 5.1 to 6.0 between 1998 and 2004, even as their headcount shrank.
stance_target: long-tenured surviving contributors intensify their workload rather than plateau, a possible analogue to top-decile creator concentration effects
quoted_support: the maintainers from the original set of July 1998 who were still active in December 2004 actually increased the number of packages they maintain.

claim: This study is explicitly a single-project case study; the authors caution it is impossible to infer general volunteer-developer behavior from one project alone, though they propose the Debian half-life as a hypothesis for validation in future research across projects.
stance_target: generalizability limits of the Debian half-life figure
quoted_support: It is impossible to infer the behavior of volunteer developers just from the study of a single project, but given the size and relevance of the Debian project, at least some conclusions can be exposed as hypothesis for validating in later research efforts.
